Fact.Name: Traditional IRA contributions (primary filer)
Fact.Description:
Screen: the IRA section, asked of the primary filer. Question: "How much did you contribute to a traditional IRA for 2025?" — the amount already contributed plus any amount you will contribute by the return due date (not including extensions). IRA Deduction Worksheet line 11a.
WHAT NOT TO ENTER (help text; each item is a rule the statute or the printed instruction states, and none of them is derivable from anything else this return collects, so the exclusion lives in the answer rather than in a later fact): * Roth IRA contributions. Those are a different question, and they are never deductible; you may instead qualify for the saver's credit. The Roth amount has its own intake in this module, /writablePrimaryFilerRothIraContributions — today it is asked only where §219(c) needs it (the spousal combined-compensation reduction), so a Roth answer is routed there and never into this box. * An employer's contribution to a simplified employee pension (SEP), and any amount contributed to a SIMPLE retirement account under section 408(p). IRC 219(b)(2) and (b)(4) put both outside this section entirely. * A rollover contribution — an amount moved from another retirement plan or IRA, described in IRC 402(c), 403(a)(4), 403(b)(8), 408(d)(3) or 457(e)(16). IRC 219(d)(2) denies the deduction for it outright; a rollover is reported on Form 1040 lines 4a and 4b instead. * Trustees' fees that were billed to you separately and paid by you for your IRA. * Repayments of qualified reservist distributions. They are not deductible here; they are entered in form8606:/writableForm8606QualifiedReservistRepayment, where the amount raises the §408(o)(2) nondeductible ceiling instead of the deduction. * Contributions you made during 2025 that you already deducted on your 2024 return. * Income from a nonqualified deferred compensation plan or a nongovernmental section 457 plan, even where it is included in box 1 of your Form W-2 or box 1 of Form 1099-NEC. That income is not compensation for IRA purposes and is subtracted for you (see /primaryFilerIraCompensation); it is not a contribution and does not belong in this answer. * If part of what you paid was a premium under an annuity or endowment contract that includes life insurance coverage, still enter the whole premium here; the part allocable to the cost of life insurance is asked separately and denied separately (/writablePrimaryFilerContributedToEndowmentContract).
Unanswered posture: complete-safe — an unanswered contribution resolves the traditional-IRA deduction $0 through the IsComplete guard on every fact that reads it, because a filer who made no IRA contribution never sees this screen. Validation: a whole dollar amount. Two cases the printed instruction sends to Pub. 590-A rather than to the worksheet, and that this dictionary does not currently distinguish either: a joint return where either spouse contributed to BOTH a traditional and a Roth IRA for 2025, and a return whose IRA deduction plus Form 8606 nondeductible contributions come to less than the total contributions made. Feeds the deduction, the section 4973 excess-contribution test and the Form 8606 nondeductible-contribution ceiling. A genuine taxpayer input: a writable, not a derived made writable. RECHARACTERIZATIONS (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-346): enter the amount after every recharacterization made by the due date. A contribution moved with its earnings by a trustee-to-trustee transfer to another kind of IRA is treated as made to the second IRA "for purposes of this chapter" (IRC 408A(d)(6)(A), 26 U.S.C. 408A, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408A&num=0&edition=2024), so an amount moved out of a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA is left out here and one moved into a traditional IRA is put in. The transfer must carry the net income (408A(d)(6)(B)(i)), and the rule applies only to the extent no deduction was allowed for the contribution to the first IRA (408A(d)(6)(B)(ii), 26 U.S.C. 408A, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408A&num=0&edition=2024). The Instructions for Form 8606 (2025) say the same (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 6).

Fact.Name: Primary filer's section 415(c)(3) compensation includible in gross income, the base of the section 219(b)(3)(B) 25 percent limit
Fact.Description: The total of W-2 box 1 over /primaryFilerW2sReportingCodeH, less the part of that box 1 excluded under section 931 or 933 (formW2s:/formW2s/*/possessionExcludedWages, not includible in gross income) and less box 11 of those W-2s (nonqualified deferred compensation, which section 219(f)(1) says is not compensation; TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-337 clarification, provisional because Treas. Reg. 1.415(c)-2 is not vendored). Wages excluded under section 911 are outside the base too (not includible in gross income); that leg is latent and not modelled, because every Form 2555 return is refused today (form2555:/knockoutFilesForm2555), the Forms W-2 that report a section 501(c)(18)(D) contribution (box 12 code H), cents kept in the addends and the total rounded once (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 23). Section 219(b)(3)(B) limits the 501(c)(18) deduction to 25 percent of "the compensation (as defined in section 415(c)(3)) includible in the individual's gross income" (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024), and section 415(c)(3)(A) defines that compensation as "the compensation of the participant from the employer for the year" (26 U.S.C. 415, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section415&num=0&edition=2024). So this is NOT the IRA compensation /primaryFilerIraCompensation: the section 219(f)(1) additions (alimony, a non-W-2 graduate stipend, self-employment earned income) are not compensation from the employer, and section 219(f)(7) restores nontaxable combat pay only for subsections (b)(1)(B) and (c) (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024), so combat pay is out. The section 415(c)(3)(D) elective deferrals are out too, because the base must be includible in gross income; box 1 already keeps the code H amount (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p525.pdf, page 10). Which employer: only the W-2s that report code H count, and wages from another employer do not (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-337, provisional; if wrong, the base would be all wages, a larger allowed amount). Source-of-record: FED-1040-IRADED-501C18BASE-038.

Fact.Name: Section 501(c)(18) contribution allowed as a section 219 deduction (primary filer)
Fact.Description: The section 219 deduction for this filer's section 501(c)(18)(D) plan contributions (W-2 box 12 code H, /primaryFiler501c18Deferrals): the lesser of the contributions, $7,000, and 25 percent of this filer's section 415(c)(3) compensation. Section 219(b)(3) caps the deduction "with respect to any contributions on behalf of an employee to a plan described in section 501(c)(18)" at "the lesser of— (A) $7,000, or (B) an amount equal to 25 percent of the compensation (as defined in section 415(c)(3)) includible in the individual's gross income" (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024). The $7,000 is a flat statutory figure with no cost-of-living clause. The compensation is /primaryFilerSection415c3CompensationFor501c18, box 1 of the Forms W-2 that report code H: section 415(c)(3) compensation includible in gross income, not the IRA compensation, so combat pay, alimony and stipends are out (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-337; FED-1040-IRADED-501C18BASE-038). TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-301 names the allowed amount, not the raw code H entry, as D. D is what comes off the IRA ceiling, what makes the filer an active participant under section 219(g)(5)(B), and what modified AGI adds back.

Fact.Name: Primary filer covered by an employer retirement plan
Fact.Description:
Whether any of the primary filer's W-2s has the Box-13 retirement-plan box checked (worksheet line 1a — "Were you covered by a retirement plan"), OR the primary filer is a self-employed active participant in a SEP, SIMPLE, or qualified retirement plan of their own.
SELF-EMPLOYED ACTIVE PARTICIPANT. Section 219(g)(5)(A) defines "active participant" as an individual who participates in a plan described in section 401(a), an annuity plan under section 403(a), a governmental plan, a section 403(b) annuity contract, a SEP (section 408(k)) or a SIMPLE (section 408(p)) — drawing NO distinction between an employee and a self-employed sponsor of the plan (a Keogh/qualified plan for a self-employed individual is itself a section 401(a) plan via section 401(c)'s "self-employed individual treated as employee" rule; SEPs and SIMPLEs are self-employed vehicles by their own design). The printed instruction states the application to this population directly rather than leaving it to be inferred from the cross-references: a filer who "were self-employed and had a SEP, SIMPLE, or qualified retirement plan" is also covered by a plan for worksheet line 1a purposes. A SEP/SIMPLE/qualified-plan contribution can only be self-employed retirement savings for someone with self-employment earned income, so this OR term fires when the primary filer has self-employment earned income AND the return's Schedule 1 line 16 is answered — the same return-level line 16 fact the compensation reduction reads. ATTRIBUTION, NAMED: unlike the DOLLAR compensation reduction (which must not double-count a return-level figure against two ceilings), this is a BOOLEAN test, so both filers may be marked covered from the same return-level line 16 answer without over- or under-stating anything — the conservative (deduction-reducing) reading this project defaults to when a return-level fact cannot be split. A filer with NO self-employment earned income cannot be the one who made a self-employed plan contribution, so this term is false for them regardless of the return-level amount.
DEDUCTIBLE 501(c)(18) CONTRIBUTIONS. Section 219(g)(5)(B) also makes an active participant of anyone "who makes deductible contributions to a trust described in section 501(c)(18)" (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024), so a third leg tests /primaryFiler501c18AllowedDeduction above $0 (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-301: the allowed deduction, not the code H entry alone). A territorial Form W-2AS, W-2GU or W-2VI with box 13 "Retirement plan" checked counts like a Form W-2 (formW2s:/primaryFilerTerritorialFormW2RetirementPlanChecked): the Form 1040 instructions read box 13 as coverage (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 96), and the W-2 instructions govern the territorial forms (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/iw2w3--2025.pdf, page 4). The reservist and volunteer-firefighter exception applies to it too. The self-employed leg tests this filer's own part of Schedule 1 line 16 (/primaryFilerOwnSchedule1Line16), so a spouse is not covered by the other spouse's plan; a blank split that is reached holds coverage as it holds compensation (lead decision GEN-01) (IRC 219(g)(5)(A), 26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024; FED-1040-IRADED-SECOMP-014).

A territorial Form W-2AS, W-2GU or W-2VI with box 13 "Retirement plan" checked counts like a Form W-2 (formW2s:/secondaryFilerTerritorialFormW2RetirementPlanChecked): the Form 1040 instructions read box 13 as coverage (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 96), and the W-2 instructions govern the territorial forms (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/iw2w3--2025.pdf, page 4). The reservist and volunteer-firefighter exception applies to it too. Unanswered resolves Complete-FALSE, so an MFS filer who has not yet answered the lived-together question keeps the $10,000 lived-with ceiling and /iraDeductionPhaseoutCeiling still RESOLVES for every filer.
This fact exists because of a measured regression, not a hypothetical, and the regression ran in the UNDER-STATEMENT direction. Reading /livedApartAllYear directly under a <Not> propagates its incompleteness: an MFS filer with /spouseLivedTogetherMonths unanswered went from Complete $10,000 to **Placeholder $89,000** — NOT to a missing value. The Switch does not stop on an Incomplete When; it falls through to the <True/> case and returns asPlaceholder, which RETAINS the value. So any consumer reading .get without checking .complete gets the $89,000 ceiling and its $79,000 floor — precisely the head start this unit's negative control exists to prevent, i.e. an UNDER-statement of tax, the direction this project refuses. Snapshots record Placeholder rows, so it would have surfaced as CHANGED, never as REMOVED: "0 removed" was never going to catch it.
The unanswered DEFAULT is deliberate and is the conservative one: $10,000 phases the deduction out sooner, so an unanswered question OVER-taxes rather than under-taxes. The $89,000 single column is reached only on an affirmative lived-apart answer, and the unanswered case resolves Complete at $10,000.

Fact.Name: IRA deduction phaseout band width (worksheet line 6 full-deduction threshold)
IRA deduction §219(g) MAGI floor — the highest MAGI still allowing a FULL deduction
Fact.Description: The phaseout's lower endpoint = /iraDeductionPhaseout- Ceiling − /iraDeductionPhaseoutBandWidth, for the primary filer's coverage/status column. Fact.Name: The §219(g) income limits provably do not reduce the primary filer's IRA deduction
Fact.Description:
True when it is PROVABLE, without resolving Form 1040 line 4b, that the §219(g) phaseout subtracts nothing from the primary filer's IRA deduction — i.e. when the largest MAGI this return could possibly produce (taxCalculations:/magiForIraDeductionUpperBound) is at or below /iraDeductionPhaseout- Floor. Note the asymmetry, which is the whole point: FALSE means "not provable", NOT "the deduction is reduced". The fact is a one-sided certificate, so the conservative answer is always false, and false leaves every consumer on the path it takes without this certificate.
The Schedule E conjunct is a REFUSAL, not a bound: scheduleE:/scheduleEActivityPresent being true makes the MAGI bound unsound (the omitted /scheduleETotalIncome addend is only exactly 0 when no Schedule E intake is claimed), so this fact refuses to certify rather than certify from an incomplete bound. See that fact's block comment.
COMPLETENESS — NOT complete-safe, and deliberately so. This fact reaches the whole income side of the return through taxCalculations:/magiForIraDeductionUpperBound, and one of those addends REFUSES on purpose: form4797:/form4797OrdinaryIncome is Result.Incomplete for a §1250 disposition or an unanswered holding period on a loss item — a World-#1 refusal rather than an unsupported §1250 recapture. In exactly those states this fact is Incomplete too, and so is form8606:/form8606Ws11Situation. The RUNTIME blast radius is nil: /totalIncome shares that same addend, so the return is already Incomplete and refuses either way — no state exists where this certificate turns a filable return into an unfilable one. But the cascade SURFACE is genuinely wider than before (the trigger transitively reads every income addend), which is disclosed on /form8606Ws11Situation rather than left to be rediscovered. NOT mef-exported. Consumed by form8606:/form8606Ws11Situation.

Fact.Name: Modified AGI for the section 219(g) phaseout (IRA Deduction Worksheet line 5)
Fact.Description: Modified AGI for the IRA phaseout: taxCalculations:/magiForIraDeduction plus the section 501(c)(18) deduction on Schedule 1 line 24f (income:/schedule1Line24fSection501c18DPensionContributionsOrZero). Section 219(g)(3)(A)(ii) figures adjusted gross income "without regard to sections 85(c), 135, 137, 221, and 911 or the deduction allowable under this section" (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024), and section 219(e)(2) makes a 501(c)(18) contribution a qualified retirement contribution deducted under this section, so it is added back with line 20. TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-301 rules this reading over the IRS worksheets, which leave line 24f subtracted (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 97). The base fact already excludes every IRA deduction; the add-back is exactly what line 24f subtracted, so a return with no line 24f entry is unchanged.

Fact.Name: IRA deduction MAGI room below the ceiling (worksheet line 6)
Fact.Description: Ceiling minus modified AGI (worksheet line 2 − line 5). Positive means partial or full deduction; zero or negative means fully phased out.

Fact.Name: IRA prorated deduction limit, before rounding (worksheet line 7, pre-round)
Fact.Description:
line6 × (flat annual dollar limitation ÷ band width). Equivalent to the worksheet percentages (70%/80% single side; 35%/40% MFJ side), expressed as limit÷range so age and filing status are encoded once.
PRORATES THE FLAT LIMIT, NOT THE 501(c)(18)-REDUCED ONE. Section 219(g)(1) reduces "each of the dollar limitations contained in subsections (b)(1)(A) and (c)(1)(A)" — the flat $7,000/$8,000 figure section 219(b)(5) defines, with no 501(c)(18) netting anywhere in that definition. Section 219(b)(1)'s 501(c)(18) reduction is a SEPARATE, later rule: a shared ceiling on the combined total of the IRA deduction and the 501(c)(18) contribution. Multiplying the ALREADY-reduced /iraAnnualContributionLimit by the phaseout ratio applies both rules in the wrong order — (limit − deferrals) × ratio is uniformly LARGER than the correct limit × ratio − deferrals whenever the ratio is below 1, so the deduction was systematically over-allowed for a filer with both a 501(c)(18) deferral and a partial phaseout. The 501(c)(18) reduction is applied AFTER proration, at /iraProratedDeductionLimitNetOf501c18 below.

Fact.Name: IRA prorated deduction limit (worksheet line 7, final)
Fact.Description: The rounded-up prorated limit, floored at $200 ("if it is less than $200, enter $200").

Fact.Name: IRA prorated deduction limit, after the section 501(c)(18) shared ceiling
Fact.Description: The worksheet line 7 result (the flat limit, prorated, rounded up to the next $10, floored at $200) minus any primary-filer section 501(c)(18)(D) elective deferral, floored at $0. Section 219(b)(1) caps the COMBINED total of the IRA deduction and the 501(c)(18) contribution at the deductible amount; that shared ceiling applies to the already-prorated worksheet result, not to the flat pre-proration limit — see /iraProratedDeductionLimitRaw's Description for the full reading and the failure direction this fact corrects. Consumed only where the phaseout actually prorates the limit (/iraDeductionLimitFromPhaseout's Switch); the not-covered and room-≥-band-width arms already read the 501(c)(18)-reduced /iraAnnualContributionLimit directly, where reducing before or after a ratio of 1 is the same number. The amount subtracted is /primaryFiler501c18AllowedDeduction, the section 219(b)(3) allowed deduction (the lesser of the code H contributions, $7,000 and 25 percent of section 415(c)(3) compensation (W-2 box 1 of the code-H W-2s, IN-337); 26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024; TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-301), not the raw code H entry.

Fact.Name: IRA deduction limit after §219(g) (worksheet line 7 result)
Fact.Description: The most the primary filer may deduct from the limit/phaseout alone, before applying compensation and the contribution actually made. Full annual limit if not covered, or if covered but MAGI room ≥ band width; $0 if MAGI is at/above the ceiling; otherwise the prorated limit.

Fact.Name: The primary filer's own part of Schedule 1 line 16
Fact.Description: The part of the return-level Schedule 1 line 16 (self-employed SEP, SIMPLE and qualified plans) that is the primary filer's own: the whole line when only the primary filer has self-employment earned income; line 16 less the spouse's answered share (scheduleSE:/writableSecondaryFilerShareOfSchedule1Line16), floored at $0, when both spouses have it; $0 when this filer has none or line 16 is $0. When both spouses have it, line 16 is above $0 and a traditional IRA contribution is answered, a blank split is held (Incomplete): a reached question left blank holds (lead decision GEN-01). Before any traditional IRA contribution is answered the split is not asked and the share is $0. IRA worksheet line 9 reduces each spouse's earned income by that spouse's own line 16 deduction (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 98; IRC 401(c)(2)(A)(v), 26 U.S.C. 401, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section401&num=0&edition=2024), and section 219(f)(2) computes each spouse separately (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024).

Fact.Name: The secondary filer's own part of Schedule 1 line 16
Fact.Description: The spouse's own part of Schedule 1 line 16: the whole line when only the spouse has self-employment earned income; the spouse's answered share (scheduleSE:/writableSecondaryFilerShareOfSchedule1Line16), floored at $0 and capped at line 16, when both spouses have it; $0 when the spouse has none or line 16 is $0. A blank split is held once reached, as on /primaryFilerOwnSchedule1Line16 (lead decision GEN-01; card 2733). Same sources as /primaryFilerOwnSchedule1Line16 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 98; 26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024).

Fact.Name: Primary filer compensation for IRA purposes (worksheet line 10)
Fact.Description:
Taxable wages (Form 1040 line 1a-1h base), plus nontaxable combat pay, plus net self-employment earned income (net earnings minus the deductible half of SE tax), plus the alimony that is the primary filer's own compensation (alimony:/primaryFilerAlimonyIraCompensation): under an instrument executed before 2019 and not modified, only alimony under a former section 71(b)(2)(A) decree or instrument incident to one counts (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024; 26 U.S.C. 71, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2016-title26-section71&num=0&edition=2016; TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-303), and on a joint return only the primary filer's part. You may not deduct more than your compensation. THIS fact is single-earner scope only — §219(c) spousal combined compensation is modeled downstream, not here: see /primaryFilerSpousalCombinedCompensation and /primaryFilerIraCompensationForDeductionLimit (the KBH-eligible deduction ceiling that actually consumes it in /primaryFilerTraditionalIraDeduction). The self-employment term is HIS OWN per-filer Schedule SE earned income (a return-level figure would inflate one spouse's §219(b)(1) ceiling by the other's self-employment earnings), read through the IRA-specific /primaryFilerSelfEmploymentEarnedIncomeForIraCompensation sibling of the Form 2441/CDCC fact so the section 1402(a)(8) minister add-back is excluded here. The worksheet's line-8/10 column is HIS, and §219(b)(1)(B) caps a deduction at "the compensation includible in the individual's gross income" — that individual's, not the couple's. THE ZERO FLOOR STAYS HERE. Form 2441 requires a self-employment LOSS to reduce earned income, so the CDCC lines moved to the unfloored siblings — but Pub. 590-A says the OPPOSITE for §219 compensation, in one sentence: "Self-employment loss. If you have a net loss from self-employment, don't subtract the loss from your salaries or wages when figuring your total compensation." The floored scheduleSE:/primaryFilerSelfEmploymentEarnedIncomeForIraCompensation keeps that zero-floor rule and separately excludes the section 1402(a)(8) minister add-back, so this term is CORRECT AS IS and is deliberately NOT re-pointed at the unfloored sibling.
STATUTORY EMPLOYEE COMPENSATION — a decision rather than a mechanical add-back, so the reasoning is recorded. THE QUESTION: round 7 routes a statutory employee's W-2 box 1 to the linked Schedule C's line 1, which takes it out of income:/primaryFilerEmployerIncomeSubtotalBase. Do those wages remain section 219 COMPENSATION after the routing? THE ANSWER IS YES, on three printed sources that agree, and the wage term now reads income:/primaryFilerEarnedIncomeBaseWithStatutoryEmployeeWages. (1) THE WORKSHEET THIS FACT IS BUILT FROM ASKS FOR BOX 1, NOT LINE 1z. IRA Deduction Worksheet line 8: "Enter the total of your (and your spouse's if filing jointly): Wages, salaries, tips, etc. Generally, this is the amount reported in box 1 of Form W-2" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 98). A statutory employee's box 1 is box 1. Nothing on that line routes through Form 1040 line 1z, so the round 7 subtraction has no purchase on it at all, and reading the reduced base here would be reading the wrong quantity rather than applying a rule. (2) PUBLICATION 590-A SAYS THE SAME THING AS A GENERAL RULE: "The IRS treats as compensation any amount properly shown in box 1 (Wages, tips, other compensation) of Form W-2, Wage and Tax Statement, provided that amount is reduced by any amount properly shown in box 11 (Nonqualified plans)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p590a.pdf, page 6). Its "What Isn't Compensation?" list is closed and names earnings and profits from property, pension or annuity income, deferred compensation, non-material-participation partnership income, CRP payments and excluded income; a statutory employee's wages are on none of them. (3) IRC 219(f)(1) IS AN INCLUSIVE DEFINITION, WHICH IS WHY THE 401(c)(2) PRONG DOES NOT DECIDE IT. "For purposes of this section, the term 'compensation' includes earned income (as defined in section 401(c)(2)). The term 'compensation' does not include any amount received as a pension or annuity and does not include any amount received as deferred compensation" (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024). The 401(c)(2) clause EXTENDS compensation to self-employment earnings; it does not narrow the wage prong, and the only exclusions the paragraph states are pensions, annuities and deferred compensation. Section 219(b)(1)(B)'s own words are "the compensation includible in the individual's gross income", and these wages ARE includible — they reach Schedule 1 line 3 through Schedule C line 31. THE ARGUMENT AGAINST, STATED AND REJECTED: a statutory employee's pay is not subject to federal income-tax withholding (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/iw2w3--2025.pdf, page 22), and the income sits on Schedule C rather than on a wage line. Neither fact appears in any of the three sources above as a condition of compensation; withholding is a collection mechanic and the schedule is a reporting route. THE DIRECTION IF THIS READING IS WRONG: the deduction ceiling is too large, taxpayer-favourable — which is why the reasoning is written out here rather than left implicit. THE DIRECTION IF THE OPPOSITE READING WERE ADOPTED is far worse and far more likely to be wrong: a filer whose ONLY earnings are statutory employee wages would have zero section 219 compensation and could not deduct an IRA contribution at all. Complete safe and equal to the raw base on every committed return, none of which checks box 13.
BOX 11 SUBTRACTION. Compensation is reduced by W-2 box 11 (nonqualified-plan distributions), summed over the primary filer's own W-2s: Pub. 590-A says box 1 counts as compensation "provided that amount is reduced by any amount properly shown in box 11" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p590a.pdf, page 6), and box 11 restates deferred compensation the individual earned in an earlier year rather than current section 219 earned income. Complete-safe $0 on every committed return, none of which answers a box 11. Box 11 is subtracted from territorial Forms W-2AS, W-2GU and W-2VI too (formW2s:/primaryFilerTerritorialNonQualifiedPlans): their box 1 is in this filer's wages, and IRA compensation is box 1 "reduced by any amount properly shown in box 11" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p590a.pdf, page 6; the W-2 instructions include the territorial forms, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/iw2w3--2025.pdf, page 4). Worksheet line 9 (self-employment earned income less Schedule 1 lines 15 and 16, floored at $0) is rounded to whole dollars as its own total: the return rounds every amount, and when adding "include cents when adding the amounts and round off only the total" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 23; TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-307). The Schedule 1 line 16 reduction is this filer's own part (/primaryFilerOwnSchedule1Line16): when both spouses are self-employed it uses the answered split of line 16 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 98; FED-1040-IRADED-SECOMP-014).

Fact.Name: Amount the primary filer chooses to deduct on Schedule 1 line 20 (§408(o)(2)(B)(ii))
Fact.Description: OPTIONAL writable — the "or a smaller amount if you choose" of IRA Deduction Worksheet line 12a / Pub. 590-A Worksheet 1-2 line 7. A genuine taxpayer election, so a writable and not a derivation: nothing else on the return reveals whether a filer who could deduct a contribution wants to. UNANSWERED MEANS DEDUCT THE WHOLE ALLOWABLE AMOUNT, which is both the default the printed worksheet assumes and the behaviour of a return that makes no election — see /primaryFilerTraditionalIraDeduction's IsComplete arm. AN ELECTED AMOUNT ABOVE THE ALLOWABLE ONE IS NOT AN ERROR AND IS NOT REFUSED: the clamp is a LesserOf, so it simply does not bind. The election can only ever reduce the deduction, which is the only direction §408(o)(2)(B)(ii) contemplates. NOT COVERED: the ORDERING choice i8606's "Line 4" instruction offers a filer with both deductible and nondeductible contributions (which of the 2025-made and 2026-made contributions to treat as nondeductible first). That is a different election, it lands on Form 8606 line 4 rather than line 1, and this fact does not answer it.

Fact.Name: Traditional IRA deduction (primary filer, Schedule 1 line 20)
Fact.Description: THE AMOUNT ACTUALLY DEDUCTED on Schedule 1 line 20: the allowable deduction (/primaryFilerTraditionalIraDeductionAllowable), reduced to the filer's elected amount when the §408(o)(2)(B)(ii) election has been answered. Unanswered ⇒ the allowable amount unchanged, which is byte-identical to a return with no election. See the block comment above for why the election lands here and not on the allowable figure. A Form 8606 line 1 designation (form8606:/writableForm8606NondeductibleContributions) given without an elected amount is itself the election not to deduct (IRC 408(o)(2)(B)(ii), 26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024; Pub. 590-A, contributions may be designated nondeductible when the return is filed, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p590a.pdf, page 16; "deduct a smaller amount and treat the rest as a nondeductible contribution", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i1040gi.pdf, page 98): the deduction is the Form 8606 line 1 starting amount (form8606:/form8606Line1ComparisonSide) less the part of the section 219(f)(6) amount that the bridge amount holds (/primaryFilerSection219f6DeductionWithinBridgeAmount: under the IN-309 amendment the section 219(f)(6) deduction can exceed the bridge when Roth contributions use up the excise room, and the excess was never in the line 1 pool, so a designation of $0 leaves the allowable deduction in place; FED-1040-IRADED-F6ROTHCAP-039) less the designated amount, net of any qualified reservist repayment, never above the allowable amount (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 9). When both an elected amount and a designation are given the elected amount sets the deduction, and form8606's line 1 knockout refuses a pair that disagree by $1 or more (obligation IRA-026, reconciliation finding).

Fact.Name: Traditional IRA deduction ALLOWABLE to the primary filer, before the §408(o)(2)(B)(ii) election
Fact.Description: The deductible traditional-IRA contribution: the amount paid to an inherited IRA comes off the contribution first (§219(d)(4); it holds while blank after a yes, TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-336); then the smallest of the §219(g) limit, the filer's compensation (KBH-adjusted per §219(c) when the primary is the lower-earning spouse — FED-1040-IRADED-KBH-001, see /primaryFilerIraCompensationForDeductionLimit), and the contribution actually made. Zero when the taxpayer has not entered a contribution amount. This is the ALLOWABLE figure; /primaryFilerTraditionalIraDeduction is the elected clamp one screen up. The split exists because §408(o)(2)(B)(ii) distinguishes ALLOWABLE from DEDUCTED and this is the allowable half — the figure term (I) is measured against and the figure the election reduces.

Fact.Name: Traditional IRA contributions (secondary filer)
Fact.Description:
Screen: the IRA section, asked of the secondary filer (MFJ spouse) — the "Spouse's IRA" worksheet column, line 11b. Question: "How much did your spouse contribute to a traditional IRA for 2025?" — the amount already contributed plus any amount they will contribute by the return due date (not including extensions).
WHAT NOT TO ENTER: the same list the primary filer's question carries, applied to the spouse's own contribution — Roth IRA contributions (the spouse's Roth amount has its own intake, /writableSecondaryFilerRothIraContributions); an employer's SEP contribution or any amount contributed to a SIMPLE retirement account under section 408(p) (IRC 219(b)(2) and (b)(4) put both outside this section); a rollover contribution described in IRC 402(c), 403(a)(4), 403(b)(8), 408(d)(3) or 457(e)(16) (IRC 219(d)(2) denies the deduction for it outright); separately billed trustees' fees; repayments of qualified reservist distributions (entered in form8606:/writableSpouseForm8606QualifiedReservistRepayment, where the amount raises the §408(o)(2) nondeductible ceiling instead of the deduction); contributions made during 2025 that were already deducted on the 2024 return; and nonqualified deferred compensation, which is not a contribution at all. Also note that a deduction for the spouse's IRA requires a joint return. An annuity or endowment premium is entered in full here, with its life-insurance portion asked and denied separately (/writableSecondaryFilerContributedToEndowmentContract).
Unanswered posture: complete-safe — absent, the spouse deduction resolves $0, leaving the primary-only behavior byte-identical. Validation: a whole dollar amount, $0 or more. A genuine taxpayer input: a writable. RECHARACTERIZATIONS (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-346): enter the amount after every recharacterization made by the due date. A contribution moved with its earnings by a trustee-to-trustee transfer to another kind of IRA is treated as made to the second IRA "for purposes of this chapter" (IRC 408A(d)(6)(A), 26 U.S.C. 408A, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408A&num=0&edition=2024), so an amount moved out of a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA is left out here and one moved into a traditional IRA is put in. The transfer must carry the net income (408A(d)(6)(B)(i)), and the rule applies only to the extent no deduction was allowed for the contribution to the first IRA (408A(d)(6)(B)(ii), 26 U.S.C. 408A, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408A&num=0&edition=2024). The Instructions for Form 8606 (2025) say the same (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8606.pdf, page 6).

Fact.Name: Spouse IRA catch-up eligible (age 50+)
Fact.Description: Whether the secondary filer is age 50 or older at the end of 2025, qualifying for the $1,000 catch-up contribution limit (Spouse's IRA column).

Fact.Name: Spouse IRA annual contribution limit (by age)
Fact.Description: The applicable 2025 annual limit for the secondary filer: $8,000 if age 50+, else $7,000 (reuses the shared standard/catch-up limit constants) — further reduced (but not below $0) by any secondary-filer section 501(c)(18)(D) elective deferrals, mirroring /iraAnnualContributionLimit (§219(f)(2) computes the maximum deduction separately for each individual). The amount subtracted is /secondaryFiler501c18AllowedDeduction, the section 219(b)(3) allowed deduction (the lesser of the code H contributions, $7,000 and 25 percent of section 415(c)(3) compensation (W-2 box 1 of the code-H W-2s, IN-337); 26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024; TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-301), not the raw code H entry.

Fact.Name: Spouse IRA deduction §219(g) MAGI ceiling (worksheet line 2, Spouse's column)
Fact.Description: The MAGI at or above which the secondary filer's deduction is fully phased out, keyed on the SECONDARY filer's own coverage. MFJ when the spouse is covered: $146,000; MFJ when the spouse is not covered (only the primary is an active participant): $246,000. The non-MFJ branch mirrors the primary fact but is unreachable — a secondary filer exists only on MFJ.

Fact.Description: The width of the secondary filer's phaseout range / proration denominator: $20,000 for the MFJ covered column (spouse is an active participant); $10,000 for the MFJ not-covered ($246,000) column.

Fact.Name: Spouse IRA deduction §219(g) MAGI floor — the highest MAGI still allowing a FULL deduction
Fact.Description: The secondary filer's mirror of /iraDeductionPhaseoutFloor — /spouseIraDeductionPhaseoutCeiling − /spouseIraDeductionPhaseoutBandWidth, keyed on the SPOUSE's own coverage column (§219(g) gives each spouse their own column even though the MAGI is joint). Same floor = ceiling − width identity, checked against the same five published Pub 590-A rows; see the primary's block comment. NOT mef-exported.

Fact.Name: The §219(g) income limits provably do not reduce the secondary filer's IRA deduction
Fact.Description: The secondary filer's mirror of /iraDeductionProvablyNotReducedByIncomeLimits — true when the largest MAGI this return could possibly produce is at or below the SPOUSE's own phaseout floor, and no Schedule E activity makes the bound unsound. Same one-sided-certificate semantics: false means "not provable", never "reduced". The MAGI bound itself is shared, not mirrored: §219(g) MAGI is a JOINT figure on MFJ (as /spouseIraDeductionMagiExcess below already reflects); only the floor differs by column. NOT mef-exported. Consumed by form8606:/spouseForm8606Ws11Situation.

Fact.Description: The spouse's ceiling minus the joint modified AGI (§219(g) MAGI is a joint figure on MFJ). Positive means partial or full deduction; zero or negative means fully phased out.

Fact.Name: Spouse IRA prorated deduction limit, before rounding (worksheet line 7, pre-round)
Fact.Description: line6 × (spouse's FLAT annual dollar limitation ÷ spouse band width). Same proration form as the primary fact, including the same correction: prorates the flat limit, not /spouseIraAnnualContributionLimit (which nets out the secondary filer's section 501(c)(18) deferral) — see /iraProratedDeductionLimitRaw's Description for the full reading. Fact.Name: Every filer who declared an endowment contract has given its life-insurance cost (flow:/flowIncomplete member)
Fact.Description:
TRUE unless a filer answered /writablePrimaryFilerContributedToEndowmentContract or /writableSecondaryFilerContributedToEndowmentContract YES and has not yet answered that filer's /writable…EndowmentLifeInsuranceCost. POPULATION, named as a conjunct of each arm: that filer's own traditional-IRA contribution is answered, so the flag reads FALSE only for a filer the endowment screen was actually shown to. It is a MEMBER of flow:/flowIncomplete's All, so a return that declares an endowment contract and then leaves the life-insurance cost blank reports itself UNFINISHED instead of leaving the filer with a deduction that cannot be computed and no reason given.
WHY IT IS HERE. The cost is a condition of allowance: with the gate YES and the cost blank, /primaryFilerEndowmentLifeInsuranceCostDenied matches no Case and resolves Incomplete, which is the truth (only the contract issuer can allocate the premium, IRC 219(d)(3)), and that incompleteness travels through the net contribution, the traditional-IRA deduction, Schedule 1 line 20, AGI and /totalTax. Incomplete alone is not the bar: nothing told the filer WHICH question is pending, because flow:/flowIncomplete's All had no iraDeduction completeness member of any kind and flow:/flowIsKnockedOut carries a Placeholder of False beneath its Any. This flag is that member. It is a completeness flag and NOT a knockout by deliberate choice, the same call the form5695 and Schedule K-1 item D members record: a blank cost is an unfinished interview, not a return that cannot be filed. The gate keeps its complete-safe posture unchanged — unanswered still means "not an endowment contract", and no return that never sees the screen moves.
COMPLETE ON EVERY INPUT, so it can never itself be the reason flow:/flowIncomplete fails to resolve: IsComplete() is Complete on every input; each All short-circuits to Complete FALSE as soon as its first conjunct (the gate's IsComplete) is false, which is every return that never answered that gate; Not() over a Complete Boolean is Complete, and an Any over two Complete Booleans is Complete.

Fact.Name: §219(c)(1)(B)(ii)(I) — the deduction ALLOWED to the secondary filer, for the primary filer's KBH combined compensation
Fact.Description: /secondaryFilerPlainTraditionalIraDeduction, reduced to her elected amount when she has answered the §408(o)(2)(B)(ii) election. THE STATUTE SAYS "ALLOWED", NOT "ALLOWABLE", and it draws the distinction itself one section over: §408(o)(2)(B)(ii) reads "an amount which (without regard to this clause) is ALLOWABLE as a deduction under section 219". Allowed = taken; allowable = eligible. A filer who elects to deduct less is ALLOWED less, so this subtrahend falls — while /secondaryFilerTraditionalIraDeductionAllowable, which term (I) of the §408(o) ceiling needs, does not. WITHOUT THIS CLAMP THE ELECTED-AWAY DOLLARS ARE COUNTED TWICE. The three subtrahends of §219(c)(1)(B)(ii) partition the spouse's IRA dollars — deducted (I), designated nondeductible (II), contributed to a Roth (III) — so a dollar she elected NOT to deduct and then designated nondeductible would be subtracted once here and once as /secondaryFiler408oNondeductibleContribution. That is taxpayer-ADVERSE (it shrinks the primary filer's compensation ceiling) and it is reachable ONLY through the §408(o)(2)(B)(ii) election writable: without an election, a fully-allowable filer's §408(o) ceiling is zero. THE COVERED BRANCH'S $0 IS THE PUBLISHED RULE, NOT A DEVIATION. A covered filer who meets Pub. 590-A's four conditions is on Appendix B, and Appendix B Worksheet 1 line 1 says to figure AGI "without taking into account any social security benefits ..., any deduction for contributions to a traditional IRA, any student loan interest deduction, or any exclusion of interest from savings bonds" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p590a.pdf, page 54) — which is exactly what this $0 does. For the covered filer who does NOT meet all four conditions (no compensation, or no contribution) Schedule 1 line 20 is $0 anyway, so the omission is arithmetically exact there too. There is no third case. Form 1040 line 6b routes that population to Appendix B Worksheet 3 on socialSecurity:/taxableSocialSecurityBenefits.
THE COMPENSATION OPERAND is the KBH-adjusted /ssbwPrimaryFilerIraCompensationForDeductionLimit. It is NOT the general /primaryFilerIraCompensationForDeductionLimit, which really would close a cycle: that fact reaches /primaryFilerSpousalCombinedCompensation, then /secondaryFilerPlainTraditionalIraDeduction, then the GENERAL /spouseIraDeductionLimitFromPhaseout, which is downstream of the §86/§219(g) MAGI this reconstruction exists to escape. You or your spouse was covered by an employer retirement plan" (lines 883-892). Appendix B's own header repeats the same four (lines 3455-3457).

It is still the right default, because Worksheet 3 without an actual Schedule 1 line 20 deduction is arithmetically IDENTICAL to Worksheet 1 — an unanswered contribution makes the deduction $0 and the two worksheets coincide, so the default costs the unanswered filer nothing.

Fact.Name: Primary filer's section 219(b)(1) CEILING, unphased — the amount a contribution may reach before any of it is a section 4973 excess
Fact.Description:
The lesser of the section 219(b)(1)(A) deductible amount (this module's /iraAnnualContributionLimit, already net of any section 501(c)(18)(D) consumption of the shared ceiling) and the section 219(b)(1)(B) compensation, taken in its section 219(c) KBH form so a lower-earning spouse is measured against the combined compensation the statute actually gives them, less the same section 501(c)(18) contribution (/primaryFilerIraCompensationLess501c18), because section 219(b)(1) caps the combined qualified retirement contributions and the IRA share is what is left. An amount paid to an inherited IRA is not measured against this ceiling: section 219(d)(4) allows it nothing, so it is added to the excess in full by /primaryFilerSection4973CurrentYearExcess (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-336). UNPHASED BY CONSTRUCTION: section 4973(b)'s flush language computes the term this stands in for without regard to section 219(g), so /iraDeductionLimitFromPhaseout is deliberately NOT read.
THIS IS THE CEILING, NOT THE ALLOWABLE DEDUCTION, and the distinction is worth the sentence. Section 4973(b)(1)(B)'s term is "the amount ALLOWABLE AS A DEDUCTION under section 219 for such contributions", which is bounded by the contribution as well as by this ceiling — min(ceiling, contribution). This fact has no contribution operand. The two are INTERCHANGEABLE FOR THE BOOLEAN TRIGGER, because C > ceiling if and only if C − min(ceiling, C) > 0, which is why /primaryFilerHasIraExcessContribution is correct as written. They are NOT interchangeable for the DOLLAR: subtracting the true (B) term always yields zero, so a successor computing the excise must subtract THIS ceiling and floor the result at $0.
DO NOT SUBSTITUTE form8606:/form8606NondeductibleLimitWithoutPhaseout. Its Name describes the same statutory idea, but its body is Round(LesserOf(limit, LesserOf(compensation, contributions))) — it carries the contribution as a third operand, so it IS the min(ceiling, contribution) form. Feeding it to the comparison below would make the test C > min(ceiling, C), which is NEVER TRUE, silently disabling /flowKnockoutIraExcessContribution.
THE COMPARISON READS THE THRESHOLD, NOT THIS FACT DIRECTLY. Section 4973(b)'s closing sentence carves a designated nondeductible contribution within a section 408(o)(5)-raised nondeductible limit out of "excess contributions", so /primaryFilerHasIraExcessContribution and /primaryFilerSection4973CurrentYearExcess both read /primaryFilerSection4973ExcessContributionThreshold, which is this ceiling plus that increase. This fact stays the pure section 219(b)(1) term, and the carve-out sits in one place where it can be read.
Not a printed line; a statutory term, consumed only by /primaryFilerSection4973ExcessContributionThreshold.

Fact.Name: Primary filer's section 4973(b) threshold — the section 219(b)(1) ceiling raised by the carve-out the closing sentence of section 4973(b) grants a section 408(o)(5) election
Fact.Description:
The amount a contribution may reach before any of it is a section 4973 excess, after the carve-out section 4973(b)'s closing sentence makes: "excess contributions" shall not include a designated nondeductible contribution that does not exceed the section 408(o)(2)(B) nondeductible limit by reason of an election under section 408(o)(5). This is /primaryFilerSection4973DeductibleAmount — the unphased section 219(b)(1) ceiling, unchanged and still the stand-in for term (B) — plus form8606:/form8606DifficultyOfCareLimitIncrease, the difficulty-of-care increase that election produces.
WHY ADDING THE INCREASE IS THE WHOLE CARVE-OUT, worked through rather than asserted. The section 408(o)(2)(B) nondeductible limit is the section 219 deduction determined without regard to section 219(g) less the deduction actually allowable, so the contribution a filer may split between a deduction and a designated nondeductible amount without producing an excess is (allowable deduction) + (nondeductible limit). Raising the nondeductible limit by the election raises that sum by exactly the increase, whatever the split between the two halves. So the threshold is the ceiling plus the increase, and the carve-out is BOUNDED: a contribution above this threshold still produces a section 4973(b)(1) excess for the part that is NOT by reason of the election, and that part is still excised and still refused. Witnessed by tests/nodes/ty2025/iraDeduction/ira-excess-beyond-the-408o5-increase-refused, which is ira-excess-compensation-limited-refused plus one key.
THE TWO OPERANDS READ DIFFERENT COMPENSATION ON PURPOSE. The ceiling reads the section 219(c) Kay Bailey Hutchison compensation, because section 4973(b)(1)(B) is a section 219 deduction amount and section 219(c) is part of section 219. The increase reads the plain per-filer compensation, because section 408(o)(5)(B) asks for "the amount of compensation includible in the individual's gross income" — that individual's. Lending a caregiver her spouse's earnings through the KBH rule would shrink the excess the increase is measured by, and so shrink an increase Congress gave her precisely for having no includible compensation of her own.
COMPLETE-SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION and it needs no guard of its own: the increase resolves $0 on every return that leaves form8606:/writableForm8606DifficultyOfCarePaymentExcluded unanswered, so an unmade election is no carve-out and this threshold is the ceiling exactly. Nothing moves on a return that makes no election.
NOT THE SECTION 408(d)(4) RELIEF, which the same closing sentence also grants and which nothing here intakes: a contribution withdrawn before the return's due date is "treated as an amount not contributed". A filer entitled to it enters a smaller Form 5329 line 15 and is refused by form5329:/form5329Line15ContradictsComputedExcess instead, which is the leg that exists for exactly that reason.
CAPPED AT THE DEDUCTIBLE AMOUNT (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-304 as amended): the threshold is the lesser of the ceiling plus the increase and the flat $7,000/$8,000 deductible amount (never below the ceiling itself), because an IRA "will not" accept contributions "in excess of the amount in effect for such taxable year under section 219(b)(1)(A)" (26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024) and Pub. 590-A allows the increase "but not above the $7,000 IRA deductible amount" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p590a.pdf, page 16). Form 5329 line 15 is then the contribution above that amount.

Adding the carve-out to the right-hand side does not disturb that equivalence: it raises both sides' ceiling by the same increase. STRICTLY GREATER: section 4973(b)(1) is "the excess (if any) of (A) ... over (B)", so a contribution exactly AT the deductible amount produces zero excess and no excise, and the return files. UNANSWERED-SAFE by the IsComplete/Switch idiom rather than a Placeholder: with no contribution answered this is Complete false, so adding it to flow:/flowIsKnockedOut's Any cannot make the master knockout less resolvable than it already was. Fact.Name: Primary filer's section 4973(b)(1) excess contribution for 2025, the dollar behind /primaryFilerHasIraExcessContribution (Form 5329 line 15)
Fact.Description:
The DOLLAR the boolean above only tested for: the section 4973(b)(1) excess of the amount contributed over the section 219 ceiling, for the current year only. The quantity is C minus the ceiling, floored at $0.
AN INHERITED-IRA PAYMENT IS EXCESS IN FULL (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-336; FED-1040-IRADED-INHERITED-006). New money paid to an IRA inherited from someone other than a spouse is an amount contributed under section 4973(b)(1)(A), and section 219(d)(4) allows no deduction for it, so its (B) amount is $0 (26 U.S.C. 4973, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section4973&num=0&edition=2024; 26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024). The excess is therefore J + max(0, (C - J) - threshold), with J /primaryFilerAmountPaidToInheritedIraDenied capped at C; the own contribution C - J keeps its own ceiling. The printed line 15 instruction measures against the contribution limit only (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i5329.pdf, page 7); the statute governs. With a yes answer and J unanswered this fact holds.
THE FLOOR IS THE BOOLEAN, not a GreaterOf (the own part C - J is also floored inside the sum). Section 4973(b)(1) says "the excess (IF ANY) of (A) ... over (B)", and /primaryFilerHasIraExcessContribution is exactly the predicate "(A) exceeds (B)" — already complete-safe false when no contribution is answered. Gating the subtraction on it gives the parenthetical's floor and reuses the shipping quantity instead of restating the comparison a second time, which is what would drift.
SUBTRACT THE THRESHOLD, NOT THE ALLOWABLE DEDUCTION, and read /primaryFilerSection4973DeductibleAmount's own Description before touching this: the true (B) term is min(ceiling, contribution), so subtracting it always yields zero. The ceiling is the operand that produces the section 4973(b)(1) dollar; what is subtracted here is that ceiling raised by the section 408(o)(5) carve-out (/primaryFilerSection4973ExcessContributionThreshold), because section 4973(b)'s closing sentence keeps a designated nondeductible contribution inside a raised nondeductible limit out of the term "excess contributions" altogether. The ceiling's Description carries the standing warning against substituting form8606:/form8606NondeductibleLimitWithoutPhaseout, which carries the contribution as a third operand and would silently zero this fact on 913 of the 969 baseline files.
THE PRINTED FORM AGREES WITH THE STATUTE HERE, checked rather than assumed (this fill's named precondition). The 2025 Instructions for Form 5329 tell the filer to enter on line 15 "the excess of your contributions to traditional IRAs for 2025 ... over your contribution limit for traditional IRAs", and send them to the line 10 instruction for that limit, which reads "your contribution limit for traditional IRAs is the smaller of your taxable compensation or $7,000 ($8,000 if age 50 or older at the end of 2025)" with the Kay Bailey Hutchison combined-compensation rule for a joint return. That is term for term /primaryFilerSection4973DeductibleAmount, so the printed line 15 and this module's section 4973 comparison measure the same ceiling.
PRIMARY FILER ONLY, DELIBERATELY, and the secondary twin is NOT authored: this dictionary renders exactly one Form 5329 and it is the primary filer's (dictionary/pdf/2025/IRS5329/en/configuration.yml pins the Part VI and Part VII fields to /primaryFiler/*), and Part III's lines and its December 31 account value are return-level singletons with no per-filer form to sit on. A secondary filer's section 4973 excise therefore still has nowhere to be reported, which is why /secondaryFilerHasIraExcessContribution survives as a leg of the narrowed knockout below.
NOT the excise itself. Six percent of this, capped by section 4973(a) at the December 31 account value, is form5329:/form5329Line17TraditionalIraExcessContributionTax, which reaches form5329:/schedule2Line8AdditionalTaxOnIrasAndOtherTaxFavoredAccounts.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 10 was answered above the unused contribution room this return derives
Fact.Description:

WHY IT REFUSES RATHER THAN PICKS A SIDE, which is the same warrant /form5329Line15ContradictsComputedExcess carries one leg down. What was missing is the other half of the line 15 treatment: the return kept the filer's figure AND filed on it. Now the entry still stands on the printed line and the return refuses, so the filer is asked rather than overruled in either direction.
THE GROUNDING IS THE WHOLE NARROWING, and without it this leg would refuse the ordinary filer who answers line 10 directly. form5329:/form5329Line10ComputedUnusedLimit is a computed $0 - NOT a derived room - until /primaryFilerTraditionalIraContributions is answered; that gate exists so an unverified section 219 ceiling is never credited as room. A $0 that means "this return has not been told" is not a figure an entry can contradict, so this fact reads the same IsComplete the computed fact's own gate reads and is Complete FALSE whenever the contribution is unanswered. THE LINE 9 CONJUNCT KEEPS IT FROM BEING A VACUOUS REFUSAL. Lines 10 to 12 reach the excise only through line 14, which subtracts line 13 from line 9 and floors at $0, so with no carry-in no entry on these lines can move any tax and there is nothing to protect.
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE. form5329:/form5329Line9TraditionalIraPriorYearExcess is complete-safe $0, both line 10 facts are complete on every return (the printed one is a nested Switch whose every arm terminates, the computed one is a complete-safe $0), and an All short-circuits on a Complete-false operand, so no return this leg does not refuse can be left unresolved.

So the leg fires only where the collection is answered AND holds at least one form; a return with none files with the entry standing. THE LINE 12 ASSUMPTION HAS ITS OWN ROUTE OUT AND THIS LEG DOES NOT CLOSE IT. Fact.Name: Flow Knockout — section 4973 excess IRA contribution
Fact.Description:
A traditional-IRA contribution over the section 219 allowable amount is not refused here: the dictionary models the 6% excise section 4973(a) imposes. dictionary/ty2025/form5329.xml ships Part III whole — line 15 (this module's /primaryFilerSection4973CurrentYearExcess), the section 4973(b)(2) carryforward on lines 9 through 14, the section 4973(a) account-value cap on line 17 — and /schedule2Line8AdditionalTaxOnIrasAndOtherTaxFavoredAccounts carries it to Schedule 2 line 8 and thence to Form 1040 line 23. So the ordinary primary-filer excess now FILES, with the excise assessed, instead of being refused.
EIGHT LEGS, in the order of the Any below. Legs (1)-(3) first, each a residue the contract names rather than a modelling gap:
(1) form5329:/form5329PartIiiExcessWithoutAccountValue — a taxable Part III excess with the December 31 account value unanswered. Line 17 taxes "the smaller of line 16 or the value of your traditional IRAs on December 31, 2025", so without that value line 17 is Incomplete and the complete-safe wrapper in front of Schedule 2 falls to $0. This is the contract's own gate, quoted: "THE RETIREMENT IS GATED ON THE INTAKE BEING ASKED, not on any further computation." Nothing asks it yet; this leg holds the population until the flow does, and retires itself when the question is put. It is keyed on the rounded six-percent excise, not the raw excess: tests/nodes/ty2025/iraDeduction/ira-excess-one-cent-over-limit-owes-no-excise-and-files pins a $0.01 excess, whose excise rounds to $0, as NOT refused; the refusal begins where the rounded excise reaches $1, pinned by the boundary-pair fixtures in the form5329 node tests.
(2) form5329:/form5329Line15ContradictsComputedExcess — the answered-contradictory intake. The filer entered a Form 5329 line 15 below the excess this return computes, or answered both a line 15 entry and the section 408(d)(4) returned-contribution relief (form5329:/form5329Line15AnsweredBesideAnsweredRelief). The relief the flush sentence of section 4973(b) grants IS intaken (form5329:/writableForm5329Line15ExcessReturnedByDueDate and /writableForm5329Line15ExcessReturnedAmount, 26 U.S.C. 4973, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section4973&num=0&edition=2024), and the computed excess already nets it, so an entry below that excess contradicts the return's own figures. The return cannot tell which is right, so it refuses instead of guessing.
(3) form5329:/spouseForm5329PartIiiExcessWithoutAccountValue - the spouse's own Part III excess with the spouse's December 31 account value unanswered: leg (1)'s twin. Section 4973(a) taxes each individual's own excess, and the 2025 Form 5329 instructions tell spouses on a joint return to complete a separate form each and include the combined tax on Schedule 2 line 8, so the spouse's excise is computed on the spouse's own Part III (form5329 /spouseForm5329Line9 through Line17, printed on the spouse's own copy) and a spouse's excess alone no longer refuses the return.
/primaryFilerHasIraExcessContribution IS NO LONGER A LEG and that is the whole narrowing. It is still read, by /primaryFilerSection4973CurrentYearExcess one fact up, which is where the comparison it makes now turns into the dollar the excise is computed from.
THREE MORE ACCOUNT-VALUE LEGS, and they are the point rather than a side effect. Leg (1) closes the silent $0 for Part III only, and the identical hole stands open on the other excess-contribution parts: each of Parts IV, V and VIII computes its 6% tax on "the smaller of [the total-excess line] or the value of your ... on December 31, 2025", each goes Incomplete when that value is unanswered, and each reaches form5329:/schedule2Line8AdditionalTaxOnIrasAndOtherTaxFavoredAccounts through a complete-safe OrZero wrapper that turns the Incomplete into a $0 with NOTHING in front of it. The three new legs are the Part III leg's twins, one per part:
(4) form5329:/form5329PartIvExcessWithoutAccountValue - section 4973(f), Roth IRAs, keyed on line 24 so the line 18 carryforward is guarded too. (5) form5329:/form5329PartVExcessWithoutAccountValue - section 4973(e), Coverdell education savings accounts, keyed on line 32 so the line 26 carryforward is guarded too. (6) form5329:/form5329PartViiiExcessWithoutAccountValue - section 4973(h), ABLE accounts, keyed on line 50, which is that part's whole base because Part VIII has no carryforward.
THIS GUARD'S PATH SAYS "IRA" AND THREE OF ITS SIX LEGS NOW DO NOT, which is a naming debt recorded here rather than paid by a rename. Section 4973 is titled "Tax on excess contributions to certain tax-favored accounts and annuities" and its subsection (a) list reaches the individual retirement account, the Archer MSA, the Coverdell education savings account, the health savings account and the ABLE account alike; the section 4973(a) cap these six legs all turn on is one sentence of that subsection, shared by every account type. So the legs belong together as a matter of law. What they do not match is a path chosen when the guard had one subject. WHAT THE THREE NEW LEGS CANNOT DO IS FIRE ON THEIR OWN INITIATIVE. This dictionary computes no Roth, Coverdell or ABLE excess: every line of Parts IV, V and VIII is a taxpayer entry, because the section 408A(c)(2), section 530(b)(1)(A)(iii) and section 529A(b)(2)(B) contribution limits are not modelled. So each new leg fires only where the filer HAS answered that part's excess line and has not answered its account value - the same pure data-completeness residue as leg (1), and the same self-retiring one. No committed scenario or fixture answers any of the three parts without also answering its December 31 value, so this widening moves nothing today.
PART IX WAS EXAMINED AND NEEDS NO LEG, which is a finding rather than an omission. Its additional tax is section 4974's, not section 4973's, and section 4974 has no account-value cap: printed lines 52a, 52b, 53a and 53b are complete-safe writable-or-$0 facts, lines 54a and 54b are computed from them, and line 55 is their sum, so form5329:/form5329PartIxExcessAccumulationTaxOrZero is complete on every return and cannot zero an excise that a missing intake would otherwise have produced. Building a Part IX twin would have been a vacuous refusal.
(7) /primaryFilerForm5329Line10ExceedsComputedUnusedLimit - an ENTERED Form 5329 line 10 above the line 10 this return computes, with a prior-year excess on line 9. The computed line 10 (form5329:/form5329Line10ComputedUnusedLimit) subtracts the contribution NET of an amount returned by the due date, because section 4973(b) treats such a contribution "as an amount not contributed" (26 U.S.C. 4973, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section4973&num=0&edition=2024; FED-1040-IRADED-LINE10ROOM-030). (8) /primaryFilerForm5329Line11ExceedsComputedDistributions - an ENTERED line 11 above the traditional IRA distributions the return's own Forms 1099-R carry into income (section 4973(b)(2)(A), 26 U.S.C. 4973, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section4973&num=0&edition=2024).
WHY LEGS (1) AND (3) REFUSE RATHER THAN COMPUTE. Line 17 is 6 percent of "the smaller of line 16 or the value of your traditional IRAs on December 31, 2025" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f5329.pdf, page 1; section 4973(a), 26 U.S.C. 4973, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section4973&num=0&edition=2024). With the December 31 value unanswered the excise has an unanswered input that can change it, so there is no number to compute; the leg holds the return until the value is given. The Form 8606 line 1 pool (form8606:/form8606Line1ComparisonSide) holds the prior-year excess only through B, the Form 5329 line 10 absorption added to IRA Deduction Worksheet line 11 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i5329.pdf, page 6), less X, which is never basis (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-342). Under the IN-309 amendment D6 is min(P - K, E') less X with no Roth term, while B is min(U - K - R, E'), so when Roth contributions use up the excise room D6 can exceed B; the excess of D6 over B is deducted although Form 5329 line 10 does not absorb it ("Part of the prior-year excess then stays an excess on Form 5329 while also being deducted", TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-309 amendment) and it was never in the pool. So this, not D6, is what comes off the pool where a Form 8606 line 1 designation sets the ordinary deduction (/primaryFilerTraditionalIraDeduction) and where form8606 bounds what can be designated. Without Roth contributions B is at least min(P - K, E'), so this equals D6 and nothing changes. A reached blank X holds it with D6 (IN-343). Derived reading recorded by the repair author for verify row FED-1040-IRADED-F6ROTHCAP-039 (ira-pilot gate D1): the package procedure (step 11) states the designation arm only for B at least D6.

Fact.Name: Closed-year excess deduction carried to the next year, C (primary filer)
Fact.Description: The part of the closed-year amount X (/primaryFilerExcessContributionDeductedInClosedYear) that this year neither applies as the section 219(f)(6)(C) reduction nor absorbs without basis: C = min(max(0, X - max(G, B)), Form 5329 line 14), where G is the deemed amount before the reduction (/primaryFilerSection219f6AmountBeforeClosedYearReduction, min(P - K, E') floored at $0) and B the bridge amount (/primaryFilerSection219f6BridgeAmount). A closed-year dollar is neutralized once, either by reducing a deemed deduction (up to G, IN-341) or by being absorbed this year without becoming basis (up to B, IN-342); the rest is still inside the carried excess, Form 5329 line 14 (form5329:/form5329Line14TraditionalIraPriorYearExcessRemaining), which caps C, and reduces the next year's section 219(f)(6) amount the same way (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-344, provisional in part: the measure max(G, B) is derived, not stated by a source). IRC 219(f)(6)(C) reduces the amount allowable by reason of paragraph (6) "for any amount allowed as a deduction under this section for a prior taxable year for which the period for assessing deficiency has expired" (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title26-section219&num=0&edition=prelim), with no limit to one later year. When the closed-year question is not reached (G is $0) X is $0 and so is C: the dollars stay not yet applied and are answered in the next year's closed-year question. A reached blank X holds C with the deduction (IN-343). It changes no line of this year's return. Emitted to the next year (the next year's intake is the matching FromPriorTaxYear writable). Source-of-record FED-1040-IRADED-F6CLOSEDYEAR-042.

Fact.Name: Section 219(f)(6) deemed additional contribution, secondary filer (MFJ spouse)
Fact.Description:
The section 219(f)(6) deemed additional contribution D6 for the secondary filer (MFJ spouse): a prior-year excess the filer is treated as contributing this year, deducted on Schedule 1 line 20 as a separate addend. Section 219(f)(2) computes each individual separately, so the spouse has its own section 219(f)(6) amount from the spouse's own Form 5329 Part III (form5329:/spouseForm5329Line9TraditionalIraPriorYearExcess and lines 11-12). IRC 219(f)(6)(A) (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024) makes it the lesser of the unused deduction room and "the amount of the excess contributions for such taxable year (determined under section 4973(b)(2) without regard to subparagraph (C) thereof)".
D6 = max(0, min(P - K, E') - X) (TAX-INTERPRETATIONS IN-309 amendment, IN-341): - min(P - K, E') is /secondaryFilerSection219f6AmountBeforeClosedYearReduction: E' is /secondaryFilerSection219f6CarriedExcess (Form 5329 line 9 less lines 11 and 12, section 4973(b)(2) without (C); 26 U.S.C. 4973, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section4973&num=0&edition=2024), and P - K is the phased maximum (/spouseIraDeductionLimitFromPhaseout against /secondaryFilerIraCompensationLess501c18, net of the allowed section 501(c)(18) deduction under IN-301) less the contribution net of the section 408(d)(4) return, "treated as an amount not contributed" (26 U.S.C. 4973, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section4973&num=0&edition=2024); - there is NO Roth term: section 219(f)(6)(A)(ii) excludes section 4973(b)(2)(C), the only clause that names Roth contributions, so U - K - R (/secondaryFilerSection219f6ExciseRoom) is the Form 5329 line 10 absorption only and the two can differ (IN-309 amendment; FED-1040-IRADED-F6ROTHCAP-039); - X is /secondaryFilerExcessContributionDeductedInClosedYear, the excess deducted in a closed year, which section 219(f)(6)(C) takes off the amount allowable by reason of this paragraph (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title26-section219&num=0&edition=prelim; IN-341; FED-1040-IRADED-F6CLOSEDYEAR-042). Reached (min(P - K, E') above $0) and blank, X holds this fact, Schedule 1 line 20 and everything downstream (IN-343). The bridge amount min(E', U - K - R) (/secondaryFilerSection219f6BridgeAmount, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i5329.pdf, page 6) stays the Form 8606 comparison-side term; the part it absorbs that is neither deducted here nor X goes to Form 8606 line 1 (IN-342).
No inherited-IRA arm: section 219(d)(4) denies the deduction for amounts paid to an inherited IRA (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024), not this deemed contribution. $0 until the traditional contribution is answered; an unanswered Form 5329 line 9 reads $0 (that posture is deferred, IRA-003). Not an MeF fact: the per-filer deduction facts carry mef="true" and this addend does not (recorded as an integration finding in the ira-deduction package reconciliation). Fenced to a married-filing-jointly return: on any other filing status it is $0 even if a secondary-filer answer is held.

Sources: IRC 219(f)(6)(A)(ii), 26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024; IRC 4973(b)(2)(A)-(B), 26 U.S.C. 4973, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section4973&num=0&edition=2024; 2025 Instructions for Form 5329, line 10, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i5329.pdf, page 6 ("The excess, if any, of Form 5329, line 9, over the sum of Form 5329, lines 11 and 12"). Fact.Name: Section 4973(b)(2)(C) room: U - K - R (secondary filer (MFJ spouse))
Fact.Description: The section 219 limit computed without regard to section 219(g) (the lesser of the deductible amount and compensation, each net of the allowed section 501(c)(18) amount, as Form 5329 line 10's ceiling already is), less this filer's net traditional contributions and Roth IRA contributions, floored at $0. Section 4973(b)(2)(C) names the Roth contribution and the flush sentence computes the limit "without regard to section 219(g)" (26 U.S.C. 4973, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section4973&num=0&edition=2024). Under IN-309 (provisional) this is the only place Roth contributions reduce the section 219(f)(6) amount. Unlike Form 5329 line 10 it does not zero for the inherited-IRA attestation: section 219(d)(4) denies the deduction for amounts paid to an inherited IRA (26 U.S.C. 219, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section219&num=0&edition=2024), not the section 219(f)(6) deemed contribution.

Feeds no federal line — the IRA deduction this module computes reads the filer's own entries, not this trustee statement — and is stored for the state and local returns and bound in the Form 5498 register.

Fact.Name: Form 5498 box 8: SEP contributions
Fact.Description: Box 8: the SEP contributions the trustee received during the year. An employer's SEP contribution is not the filer's own IRA deduction, and no federal line on this return reads this box. Unanswered it is complete-safe. Feeds no federal line — the IRA deduction this module computes reads the filer's own entries, not this trustee statement — and is stored for the state and local returns and bound in the Form 5498 register.

Fact.Name: Form 5498 box 15b: code(s) for the specified assets
Fact.Description: Box 15b: the code or codes the trustee printed for the box 15a assets, chosen from /form5498SpecifiedAssetCodeOptions, whose options are the printed letters themselves (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/f5498--2025.pdf, page 4). A MultiEnum because the box holds "Code(s)": the instructions allow at most two, and code H when more than two apply (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099r--2025.pdf, page 26); the graph does not enforce the two-code cap, so the filer copies whatever the trustee printed. Unanswered it is complete-safe. Feeds no federal line — the IRA deduction this module computes reads the filer's own entries, not this trustee statement — and is stored for the state and local returns and bound in the Form 5498 register.
